nameStory: Painted-cup paintbrush gets its vibrant name from its brilliant scarlet-orange flower bracts that look exactly like an artist's paintbrush dipped in bright red paint. Early settlers and Native Americans both saw these fiery blooms dotting meadows and imagined a giant artist had been painting the landscape, leaving their brushes scattered across the prairie.
description: Painted-cup paintbrush is a striking wildflower that grows 1-2 feet tall with clusters of what appear to be bright red-orange flowers at the top. The real flowers are actually small and greenish-yellow, hidden inside those showy scarlet bracts (modified leaves) that steal all the attention. This biennial plant grows from a rosette in its first year, then sends up its colorful flowering stem in the second year before completing its life cycle.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Brilliant scarlet-orange bracts surround small, tubular greenish-yellow flowers that peek out like tiny beaks. The bracts feel papery and are deeply lobed, creating the classic paintbrush appearance.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Lower leaves are lance-shaped and smooth-edged, while upper leaves become increasingly lobed and tinged with the same red-orange color as the bracts. All leaves feel slightly rough and are arranged alternately on the stem.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms a low rosette of leaves in its first year, then sends up a single unbranched stem 12-24 inches tall topped with the colorful flower cluster in its second year.

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small brown capsules develop after flowering, splitting open to release tiny seeds that rattle softly when the dried stem is shaken in late summer.

habitat: Look for painted-cup paintbrush in open prairies, meadows, and rocky glades with good drainage and full sun to partial shade. In New England, it's most likely found in moist woodlands, along stream edges, and in natural clearings. It prefers neutral to slightly alkaline soils and is often associated with native grasses and other prairie remnant species.

seasonality.spring: First-year plants appear as small rosettes of lance-shaped leaves close to the ground, while second-year plants send up their flowering stems.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming occurs from late May through July, when the spectacular scarlet bracts are most vibrant and visible from quite a distance.
seasonality.fall: Seed capsules mature and split open, releasing seeds. The colorful bracts fade to brown and the whole plant begins to die back after completing its two-year lifecycle.
seasonality.winter: Plants are dormant, with only first-year rosettes potentially visible under snow cover, though they're easily overlooked.

funFact: Painted-cup paintbrush is actually a sneaky plant thief that taps into the roots of neighboring grasses and wildflowers to steal water and nutrients, making it what botanists call a 'hemiparasite' - it can photosynthesize on its own but supplements its diet by parasitizing other plants!
confusionNotes: The brilliant red-orange bracts are so distinctive that painted-cup paintbrush is rarely confused with other plants when in bloom. Out of bloom, the lance-shaped leaves might be overlooked among other prairie plants, but the alternately arranged, increasingly lobed upper leaves help distinguish it.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'paintbrush,' this plant is completely unrelated to the yellow desert paintbrushes commonly seen in western wildflower photos - those belong to a different genus entirely, though they're in the same plant family and have a similar parasitic lifestyle.
compareHints: Painted-cup paintbrush differs from its relative northern paintbrush by its brilliant scarlet-red bracts (northern paintbrush has pale yellow to greenish-white bracts) and its preference for more eastern habitats. Northern paintbrush is extremely rare in New England and tends to prefer cooler, more northern climates, while painted-cup paintbrush, though still uncommon, is more likely to be encountered in our region's prairies and open woodlands.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Northern paintbrush differs from its close relative painted-cup paintbrush by its preference for high-elevation alpine habitats rather than low-elevation meadows and prairies.
